modules.nm: Who can act: users, groups, roles
modules.goal: Tell a user, a group and a role apart, and say which one an exam scenario needs.

blocks.x: IAM answers one question for every AWS API call ever made: **is this caller allowed to do this?** Everything else in this subject is detail hanging off that. An identity is *who is asking*; a policy is *what that identity may do*.
The three identities

head: Identity
What it is
Credentials
Use it for
rows: One person or one application, permanent
Password for the console, access keys for the CLI/SDK — both long-lived
A human who signs in. Almost nothing else
A bag of users you attach policies to
None — a group is not an identity that can act
Managing permissions for many people at once
None stored. STS mints temporary keys on assumption
EC2, Lambda, ECS, another AWS account, a federated user

blocks.x: A group is not a principal. It cannot be named in a trust policy, it cannot own credentials, and groups cannot be nested inside other groups. If an answer says "add the group as the principal", it is wrong.
Why roles win almost every scenario

A user's access keys live forever until someone rotates them. A role's credentials come from **STS**, carry an expiry, and are fetched automatically — nothing is stored on disk, in an AMI, or in an environment variable, so nothing can leak from there.

x: EC2 / Lambda / ECS needs S3
It assumes its attached role
STS returns temporary keys
Call is signed and allowed
Keys expire and refresh
blocks.cap: No human, no stored secret, no rotation job.

blocks.x: The root user

x: Created with the account, identified by the sign-up email, and holds unrestricted power that **no IAM policy can limit**.
Enable MFA on it immediately — hardware MFA for anything serious.
Delete its access keys outright. Do not rotate them; root should have none at all.
Use it only for the handful of tasks that require it: closing the account, changing the support plan, some billing settings.

blocks.x: "Give the developer root access so they can finish quickly" is never the answer, in any question, ever. Create an IAM role or user with the permissions actually needed.

o.t: An IAM role granting the S3 read permissions
An IAM group containing the instance
An IAM user's access keys written into a file on the instance
The root user's access keys, stored as an environment variable

checks.x: Compute that calls an AWS API gets a role. STS hands the instance temporary credentials that rotate on their own, so there is no long-lived secret sitting on disk to leak. Access keys on an instance are the classic wrong answer, root keys are worse, and a group cannot contain an instance at all.

checks.q: Which statement about IAM groups is correct?

o.t: A group can be assumed the same way a role can
A group can contain users, but groups cannot be nested and cannot be a principal
A group has its own access keys that its members share
A group can contain both users and EC2 instances

checks.x: A group is purely a convenience for attaching policies to many users at once. It holds no credentials, cannot be assumed, cannot be named as a principal in a trust policy, and cannot be put inside another group.

checks.q: Which task genuinely requires the root user?

o.t: Attaching a policy to a developer's IAM user
Launching an EC2 instance in a new region
Creating an S3 bucket for production logs

checks.x: Closing the account is one of the few operations reserved for root. Day-to-day work — policies, EC2, S3 — belongs to an IAM user or role with the right permissions. Root should be locked away behind MFA with no access keys at all.

checks.q: Why are role credentials considered safer than an IAM user's access keys?

o.t: They cannot be used by the AWS CLI
They are longer, so they are harder to guess
They work only inside a single VPC
They are issued by STS, expire on their own, and are never stored on the instance

checks.x: The safety comes from the credentials being temporary and never written down. STS issues them on assumption with a fixed expiry and the SDK refreshes them automatically, so a leaked copy is useless within hours — unlike an access key that stays valid until a human rotates it.

modules.nm: What they may do: policies and evaluation
modules.goal: Read a policy document and work out whether a specific call is allowed or denied.

blocks.x: A policy is a JSON document made of statements. Each statement has an **Effect** (Allow or Deny), an **Action**, a **Resource**, and optionally a **Condition**. That is the whole language.

blocks.cap: Read GetObject on one bucket's objects — but only when the caller authenticated with MFA.

blocks.x: Two places a policy can hang

items: Attached to a user, group or role
Cannot grant anything to a caller in another account on its own
Attached to the resource — S3 bucket policy, KMS key policy, SQS queue policy
The only way to grant cross-account access without assuming a role

blocks.x: Evaluation logic — the part that is tested constantly

x: Start from an implicit **deny**. Nothing is allowed by default.
Look for an explicit **Deny** anywhere at all — identity policy, resource policy, SCP, permissions boundary. If one applies, the call fails and nothing can override it.
Look for an explicit **Allow**. If one applies and no Deny did, the call succeeds.
No Allow found? The implicit deny stands and the call fails.

blocks.x: Explicit Deny beats every Allow, always, no matter how many Allows there are or where they came from. This single rule answers a surprising number of exam questions.

Account A resource policy names B's principal
Call succeeds

o.t: The call is denied — an explicit Deny cannot be overridden by any Allow
The call is allowed only from inside a VPC
The call is allowed, because the identity policy is more specific
The two policies cancel out and the call is retried

checks.x: An explicit Deny anywhere in the evaluation — identity policy, resource policy, SCP or permissions boundary — ends the decision immediately. No number of Allow statements can rescue the call.

checks.q: An IAM role has no policy that mentions DynamoDB at all, and nothing denies it either. Can the role call DynamoDB?

o.t: Yes, but only for read actions
No — with no explicit Allow, the implicit deny stands
Only if the table is in the same region

checks.x: IAM starts from an implicit deny. Silence is not permission: without a statement that explicitly allows the action, the call fails even though no Deny was written anywhere.

checks.q: Team B in Account B needs to read an S3 bucket owned by Account A. What is required?

o.t: Making the bucket public so both accounts can reach it
A bucket policy in Account A naming Account B's principal only
A bucket policy in Account A naming the principal, and an IAM policy in Account B allowing the S3 actions
An IAM policy on the role in Account B only

checks.x: Cross-account access needs both halves. The resource-based bucket policy in the owning account has to name the calling principal, and the calling identity's own policy has to permit the S3 actions. Doing one side leaves the request denied on the other, and making the bucket public is never the fix.

checks.q: Which policy type can grant access to a principal in a different AWS account without that principal assuming a role?

o.t: A customer managed policy attached to a local role
An inline policy on a local IAM user
A resource-based policy such as an S3 bucket policy

checks.x: Only a resource-based policy can name an external principal directly, which is what lets an S3 bucket, SQS queue or KMS key be shared across accounts. Identity-based policies of every flavour only describe what their own identity may do.

modules.goal: Diagnose why a role assumption failed, and design cross-account access correctly.

blocks.x: Assuming a role is a call to **STS**, the Security Token Service. It returns three things — an access key, a secret key and a **session token** — with an expiry. Anything without that session token is not a role credential.
A role has two policies, and they are not the same policy

items: Names principals — an account, a role, a service such as ec2.amazonaws.com
A failure here means the assumption itself is refused
Answers: *what may I do once assumed?*
A failure here means you got the credentials and then got AccessDenied

blocks.x: Failed to assume the role at all → fix the **trust policy**. Assumed it fine, then got AccessDenied on the API call → fix the **permission policy**. Which failure you were told about tells you which document is wrong.
The cross-account pattern

x: In the target account, create a role whose **trust policy** names the source account (or a specific role in it).
Give that role a permission policy covering exactly what the caller needs.
In the source account, allow the calling identity to run `sts:AssumeRole` on that role's ARN.
The caller assumes the role, receives temporary credentials, and acts **as a principal of the target account**.

blocks.x: A third-party vendor whose tooling runs in their own AWS account should assume a cross-account role in yours. Creating an IAM user for the vendor and emailing them access keys is the wrong answer even though it works.

Mechanism
Notes

Also controls CloudWatch Logs access and VPC attachment
Per-task, distinct from the EC2 instance role underneath it
A CI system assumes a role with no stored keys at all

blocks.x: `aws sts get-caller-identity` prints exactly which identity the current credentials belong to. It is the fastest way to prove whether you are running as the role you think you are.

checks.q: An application can assume its role, but every S3 call then returns AccessDenied. Which document should you fix?

o.t: The permission policy on the role
The trust policy on the role

checks.x: The assumption succeeded, so the trust policy already allows the caller. What fails afterwards is the action itself, which is governed by the role's permission policy. Trust policy failures stop you before any credentials are issued.

checks.q: What does STS return when a role is assumed?

o.t: A temporary access key, secret key and session token with an expiry
A console password for the role

checks.x: Role credentials are a triple — access key, secret key and session token — and they expire. The session token is what marks them as temporary; a credential set without one is a long-lived IAM user key.

checks.q: An external vendor's software runs in the vendor's own AWS account and needs to read your CloudWatch metrics. What should you set up?

o.t: An IAM user in your account whose keys you send to the vendor
A shared root password for the two accounts
A role in your account whose trust policy names the vendor's account, which their role assumes
Public read access on the metrics

checks.x: Cross-account access is a role in the account that owns the data, trusted to the account that needs it. Nothing long-lived is ever handed over, and access is revoked by editing one trust policy rather than by chasing down a key someone copied.

checks.q: On an EC2 instance, what is an instance profile?

o.t: A saved set of access keys stored in the AMI
The wrapper that attaches an IAM role to the instance

checks.x: An instance profile is a thin container the console creates automatically so a role can be attached to EC2. Whenever a question says instance profile, read it as the IAM role the instance is running with.

modules.nm: MFA, password policy and the audit tools
modules.goal: Apply the account-hardening answers the exam expects, and name the tool that proves it.

blocks.x: A block of questions in this subject is really asking *what does a well-run account look like?* The answers are always the same handful of controls.
Multi-factor authentication

x: Virtual MFA — an app on a phone. Hardware key or U2F security key for higher assurance.
MFA on root is non-negotiable, and on every privileged human identity.
MFA can be **required by policy**, not merely suggested, using the condition key `aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent`.
Long-lived IAM user keys do not carry the MFA flag. The user calls `sts:GetSessionToken` while authenticated with MFA, and uses the temporary credentials that come back.

blocks.x: "Force MFA for these CLI actions" → deny the actions unless `aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent` is true, then have the user obtain temporary credentials with `GetSessionToken`. You cannot make the CLI prompt for a code by itself.
Password policy
Account-wide and configurable: minimum length, required character types, expiry and rotation, reuse prevention, and whether users may change their own password.
The two audit tools people mix up

head: Tool
Scope
Answers the question
rows: Who has keys, how old are they, who has MFA, who never signs in?
One user, group, role or policy
Which services has this identity actually used, and when?

blocks.x: Access Advisor is the tool for trimming an over-permissive policy, because it shows services granted but never touched. The credential report is for finding stale keys and missing MFA. Picking the wrong one is a common trap.
The best-practice answers

x: Least privilege: grant the permissions the job needs, then widen only if something breaks.
One IAM user per human, never a shared login.
Roles for anything that is not a human.
Rotate what must exist, and delete what should not exist at all — starting with root access keys.

checks.q: A policy must require multi-factor authentication for a set of sensitive CLI actions. What is the mechanism?

o.t: Deny the actions unless aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent is true, and have the user get temporary credentials with GetSessionToken
Ask the user to type the MFA code as an argument to every command
It cannot be done outside the console
Enable MFA on the root user and nothing else is needed

checks.x: MFA is enforced as a policy condition. Because a long-lived access key carries no MFA flag, the user first authenticates with MFA through GetSessionToken and then uses the temporary credentials, which do carry it.

checks.q: Which tool shows, for a single role, which services it was granted but has never actually called?
checks.x: Access Advisor reports last-accessed data per identity, which is exactly what you need to trim a policy down to least privilege. The credential report is account-wide and describes credentials, not service usage.

checks.q: Which finding would the IAM credential report reveal?

o.t: Which EC2 instances are running without a role
That several users have access keys older than a year and no MFA device

checks.x: The credential report is a per-user inventory of credentials: password age, key age, whether keys are active and whether MFA is enabled. Public buckets and failed API calls come from entirely different services.

checks.q: What is the recommended handling of root user access keys?

o.t: Store them in an S3 bucket for the team
Share them with the on-call engineer
Delete them so the root user has no access keys at all

checks.x: Root should have no programmatic credentials to rotate in the first place. Delete them, protect root with MFA, and do everyday work through IAM roles and users that can actually be constrained by policy.

modules.goal: Predict which credentials a call will use, and harden instance metadata.

blocks.x: The CLI and every SDK look for credentials in a fixed order and stop at the first source that produces them. Knowing the order explains almost every "why is it using the wrong account?" question.

~/.aws/credentials
~/.aws/config
Container credentials (ECS task role)
Instance metadata (EC2 role)
blocks.cap: First match wins — a stale environment variable silently beats the instance role.

blocks.x: An EC2 instance with an attached role needs **zero** stored credentials. The SDK reads them from the instance metadata service at `169.254.169.254` and refreshes them before they expire.
IMDSv1 versus IMDSv2

head: IMDSv1
IMDSv2

A PUT first obtains a session token, which every later request must carry
A server-side request forgery bug can reach it
Token requirement blocks the usual SSRF path

blocks.x: If a question mentions stolen instance credentials through an application vulnerability, the hardening answer is enforcing IMDSv2 — not a security group change. Metadata never leaves the instance, so no network rule touches it.

`aws sts get-caller-identity` proves which identity is really in use.
**CloudShell** is a browser shell already holding your console identity — no keys to configure, and it is region-based.

checks.q: An EC2 instance has an IAM role attached, but the CLI on it keeps acting as a different identity. What is the most likely cause?

o.t: Credentials earlier in the chain — environment variables or ~/.aws/credentials — are being found first
The role is missing a trust policy
The instance is in a private subnet

checks.x: The chain stops at the first source that yields credentials, and the instance role sits last. A leftover environment variable or credentials file silently wins, which is why get-caller-identity is the first troubleshooting step.

checks.q: An application vulnerability was used to read EC2 instance credentials from the metadata service. What hardening step addresses this directly?

o.t: Remove the instance from its security group
Enforce IMDSv2 so metadata requests require a session token
Move the instance to a public subnet

checks.x: IMDSv2 requires a PUT to obtain a token before any metadata read, which defeats the server-side request forgery pattern used to reach the metadata endpoint. Security groups are irrelevant here — the metadata service is local to the instance.

checks.q: Which command confirms which identity the CLI is currently using?
checks.x: get-caller-identity returns the account, the ARN and the user or role ID behind the credentials in use. It answers "who am I right now", which listing profiles or users cannot.

checks.q: What is AWS CloudShell?

o.t: A service that stores long-lived access keys for a team
A local installer for the AWS CLI
A managed EC2 instance you pay for hourly
A browser-based shell that already carries your console identity, with no keys to configure

checks.x: CloudShell is a terminal in the console running as the identity you signed in with, so the CLI is pre-authenticated. It is region-based and needs no access keys, which makes it the quick answer for one-off commands.

recap.x: The one rule everything else hangs off

Every AWS API call is evaluated the same way: **implicit deny → explicit Deny wins → explicit Allow → otherwise denied.** When a question describes an unexpected AccessDenied, walk that ladder before anything else.

final.q: A Lambda function must write objects to an S3 bucket in the same account. Which approach is correct and most secure?

o.t: Attach an execution role to the function with a policy allowing s3:PutObject on the bucket
o.w: Correct — the execution role is how Lambda authenticates, and its credentials are temporary and rotated automatically.

o.t: Make the bucket public so the function can write without credentials
o.w: Public write removes access control entirely and is never the answer to a permissions question.

o.t: Create an IAM user and put its access keys in the function's environment variables
o.w: Long-lived keys in environment variables are readable by anyone who can view the function configuration, and they never expire on their own.

o.t: Use the root account's access keys inside the function code
o.w: Root credentials cannot be constrained by any policy, so this maximises blast radius instead of reducing it.

final.x: Compute that needs AWS access gets a role. The execution role's permission policy names the exact action and bucket, credentials come from STS with an expiry, and nothing sensitive is stored in the function.

final.q: A developer's IAM policy allows s3:* on all buckets, but a permissions boundary on the same user allows only DynamoDB actions. What can the developer do in S3?

o.t: Read but not write in S3
o.w: A boundary does not grade actions into read and write; S3 is simply not within it.

o.t: Nothing in S3 — the boundary caps what their policies can grant
o.w: Correct — effective permissions are the intersection of the identity policy and the boundary, and S3 is outside the boundary.

o.t: Everything in S3 only from the console
o.w: The console and the API are evaluated by the same policy engine, so the access path changes nothing.

o.t: Everything in S3, because the identity policy grants it
o.w: A boundary is not overridden by a broad identity policy; it is a ceiling applied on top of it.

final.x: A permissions boundary never grants anything — it limits what the identity's own policies are able to grant. Where the two do not overlap, there is no access, which is what makes boundaries safe for delegated administration.

final.q: An S3 bucket policy explicitly denies a role, while that role's identity policy allows s3:GetObject. What is the result of a GetObject call?

o.t: Allowed, because the two statements cancel out
o.w: Policies never cancel out — an explicit Deny is absolute.

o.t: Denied only if the object is encrypted
o.w: Encryption affects KMS permissions, not the outcome of this Deny.

o.t: Denied — an explicit Deny in any applicable policy wins
o.w: Correct — explicit Deny is evaluated first and terminates the decision regardless of source.

o.t: Allowed, because identity policies take precedence over resource policies
o.w: There is no precedence of identity over resource policies; both feed the same evaluation.

final.x: The evaluation order is implicit deny, then explicit Deny, then explicit Allow. Because a Deny was found, evaluation stops there — this is the rule that decides most surprising AccessDenied scenarios.

final.q: An application on EC2 uses an instance role, but after a deployment it started making calls as an unrelated IAM user. What should you check first?

o.w: Security groups control network traffic and have nothing to do with which identity signs a request.

o.t: Whether the bucket is in the same region
o.w: Region affects endpoints, not which credentials the SDK picked up.

o.t: The role's trust policy, which must have expired
o.w: Trust policies do not expire; had it been a trust problem, no credentials would have been issued at all.

o.t: Environment variables and ~/.aws/credentials on the instance, which sit earlier in the credential chain
o.w: Correct — the SDK stops at the first credential source it finds, and both of those precede instance metadata.

final.x: Credential resolution is ordered: CLI options, environment variables, the credentials file, the config file, container credentials, then instance metadata. A leftover file or exported variable silently overrides the role.

final.q: Security requires that deleting objects from a sensitive bucket only succeeds when the caller has authenticated with MFA. How is this enforced?

o.t: A policy condition denying the action unless aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent is true
o.w: Correct — MFA is expressed as a condition key, and the caller supplies MFA-backed temporary credentials through GetSessionToken.

o.t: Adding the users to a group named MFA-Required
o.w: Group membership carries no MFA signal; only the condition key does.

o.t: Setting a password policy that requires rotation
o.w: Password rotation is unrelated to whether a given API call carried MFA.

o.t: Enabling MFA on the root user
o.w: Root MFA protects root alone and says nothing about what other identities may do.

final.x: The condition key aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent is the enforcement mechanism. Long-lived keys never carry it, so the user calls sts:GetSessionToken while authenticated with MFA and uses the returned temporary credentials.

final.q: Which design correctly gives fifty engineers access to twelve AWS accounts?

o.t: An IAM user for each engineer in each account
o.w: Six hundred user records is an administrative and offboarding disaster, and it is the classic wrong answer.

o.t: IAM Identity Center with permission sets assigned to groups
o.w: Correct — Identity Center assigns permission sets centrally and the engineers assume roles in each account.

o.t: Cognito user pools federated into each account
o.w: Cognito is for the end users of an application you built, not for workforce access to AWS accounts.

o.t: One shared IAM user per account with the password in a wiki
o.w: Shared credentials destroy attribution and cannot be revoked per person.

final.x: Workforce identity across many accounts is what IAM Identity Center exists for: one assignment of a permission set, roles assumed per account, and offboarding handled in one place.

final.q: A partner company's application, running in their own AWS account, needs read access to your DynamoDB table. What should you create?

o.t: An IAM user in your account whose access keys you email to the partner
o.w: Emailed long-lived keys cannot be rotated reliably and will outlive the relationship.

o.t: A public endpoint in front of the table
o.w: Exposing a datastore publicly is never the intended answer to an access-control requirement.

o.t: A role in your account trusting the partner's account, which their application assumes
o.w: Correct — a cross-account role with a trust policy naming their account keeps the credentials temporary and revocation instant.

o.t: A copy of the table in the partner's account, refreshed nightly by hand
o.w: Manual copying introduces staleness and does not address access control at all.

final.x: Cross-account access is always a role in the account that owns the resource, trusted to the account that needs it, with the caller permitted to run sts:AssumeRole. Revoking access is then a single trust policy edit.

final.q: A security review must identify every IAM user whose access keys are more than a year old and who has no MFA device. Which tool produces this?

o.w: Bucket policies describe access to S3 objects and say nothing about IAM users.
Instance metadata serves credentials to one EC2 instance; it is not an audit tool.
Access Advisor reports which services an identity has used, not the state of its credentials.
Correct — the credential report is an account-wide CSV listing key age, key state, password age and MFA status per user.

final.x: The credential report is the account-wide credential inventory, which makes it the right tool for stale keys and missing MFA. Access Advisor answers a different question — what an identity actually used — and is the tool for trimming permissions.

final.q: Which measure most directly reduces the risk of an application vulnerability being used to steal an EC2 instance's role credentials?

o.w: Correct — IMDSv2 requires a session token obtained by a PUT, which breaks the server-side request forgery path to the metadata endpoint.

o.t: Moving the instance into a public subnet
o.w: Subnet placement changes routing, not local access to the metadata service.

o.t: Disabling the instance profile and storing keys in a file instead
o.w: Replacing rotating temporary credentials with a static key file makes the exposure permanently worse.

o.t: Attaching a second IAM role to the instance
o.w: An instance can only have one role attached, and a second one would not change how metadata is reached.

final.x: Instance credentials are served locally by the metadata service, so no network control protects them. IMDSv2's token requirement is the specific hardening for the SSRF pattern that leaks them.

final.q: A startup wants its mobile app's customers to sign in and then upload directly to S3 with temporary AWS credentials. Which service fits?

o.t: An IAM user created per customer at sign-up
o.w: Creating an IAM user per customer hits account limits and leaves permanent credentials everywhere.

o.t: Amazon Cognito, with an identity pool issuing temporary credentials
o.w: Correct — Cognito user pools handle app sign-in and identity pools exchange that identity for scoped temporary AWS credentials.

o.t: IAM Identity Center with a permission set per customer
o.w: Identity Center is built for workforce access across accounts, not for consumers of an application.

o.t: The root user with MFA enabled
o.w: Root is a single account-level identity and can never represent application users.

final.x: The cue is who signs in. Customers of an application are Cognito's job — the user pool authenticates them and the identity pool trades that token for temporary credentials scoped by an IAM role.

Multi-Attach works within one Availability Zone and is not a replication feature.

o.t: Move the volumes into an EFS file system
o.w: EFS is a different service; moving data into it does not replicate EBS volumes.

o.t: Attach the volumes to instances in the second region
o.w: Volumes cannot be attached across zones, let alone across regions.

final.x: Cross-region snapshot copy is the standard EBS disaster recovery answer, and Data Lifecycle Manager or AWS Backup can run it on a schedule.

final.q: An application needs 16,000 IOPS from a 100 GB volume, and the team wants the lowest cost that meets it. Which choice fits best?

o.t: gp2, sized up until the IOPS target is reached
o.w: gp2 ties IOPS to size, so hitting the target means buying a much larger volume than needed.

o.t: gp3, with IOPS provisioned independently of the volume size
o.w: Correct — gp3 lets you buy the IOPS you need without paying for capacity you do not.
st1 is an HDD built for sequential throughput and cannot deliver that many IOPS.
sc1 is the coldest, slowest option and Fast Snapshot Restore does not change its performance.

final.x: The gp3 to gp2 difference is exactly this: gp3 decouples performance from capacity. Paying for a large gp2 volume only to reach an IOPS number is the pattern gp3 was introduced to remove.

final.q: Instances launched by Auto Scaling take six minutes to become healthy because their user data installs and configures software every time. What reduces the launch time most?

o.w: A bigger instance shortens the install a little but still repeats all of it.
Network interfaces have no effect on boot time.

o.t: Create a custom AMI with the software already installed and launch from it
o.w: Correct — baking the image does the installation once instead of on every launch.
Faster storage does not remove the work of downloading and configuring packages.

final.x: A golden AMI turns repeated launch-time work into build-time work, which is the standard answer when scale-out is too slow. User data then handles only the small per-instance differences.

final.q: An EFS file system holds many files that are never read after their first week, and the bill is dominated by storage. What should be configured?

o.t: A second mount target in each subnet
o.w: Mount targets are about reachability, not cost.
Provisioned throughput increases cost rather than reducing it.
Performance mode affects latency and parallelism, not storage price.

o.t: A lifecycle policy that moves files to the Infrequent Access class
o.w: Correct — lifecycle management moves untouched files to a much cheaper class automatically.

final.x: EFS Infrequent Access trades a per-read charge for far cheaper storage, and the lifecycle policy applies it based on how long a file has gone untouched — the standard answer for a storage-heavy EFS bill.

final.q: A workload needs the fastest possible local disk for temporary shuffle files that can be regenerated. Which storage should be used?

o.t: Instance store volumes on the instance
o.w: Correct — instance store is physically attached, giving the highest IOPS, and the data is regenerable so its volatility does not matter.
EFS adds network file system overhead, which is the wrong direction for scratch data.
EBS is network attached and slower than local disk for this pattern.
Multi-Attach adds sharing complexity for data that only one instance uses.

final.x: Two facts decide it: the requirement asks for maximum speed, and the data is explicitly rebuildable. That combination is the one case where instance store's volatility is acceptable.

final.q: A team must share an encrypted EBS snapshot with a partner AWS account. The snapshot was encrypted with the default EBS key. What has to change?

o.t: Decrypt the snapshot and share it unencrypted
o.w: Removing encryption to enable sharing defeats the control the encryption exists to provide.

o.t: Copy the snapshot and re-encrypt it with a customer managed KMS key that the partner account may use
o.w: Correct — AWS-managed keys cannot be shared, so the snapshot must be re-encrypted under a key whose policy grants the partner access.
Making an encrypted snapshot public is not possible and would be a serious exposure in any case.

o.t: Convert the snapshot into an instance store volume
o.w: Snapshots and instance store are unrelated; there is no such conversion.

final.x: The blocking constraint is the key, not the snapshot. Default service keys have no shareable key policy, so cross-account sharing always requires a customer managed key granted to the other account.

blocks.x: A load balancer spreads traffic across healthy targets and gives clients one stable name. AWS has three, and they operate at different layers.

**One static IP per AZ, and Elastic IPs are supported**

Sending traffic through firewalls and inspection appliances

blocks.x: Two phrases decide almost every load balancer question. **"A static IP address"** or **"UDP"** means NLB. **"Route by URL path or hostname"** means ALB.
What only the ALB can do

x: Rules by **path** (`/api/*` to one target group), **host** (`shop.example.com`), header, query string or HTTP method.
Invoke a **Lambda function** as a target.
Redirect HTTP to HTTPS, and return fixed responses without a backend.
Authenticate users through Cognito or an OIDC provider before traffic reaches the target.
Pass the client's address in the **X-Forwarded-For** header — the target sees the load balancer's IP otherwise.

x: Handle **UDP** and raw TCP.
Give you a **static IP per Availability Zone**, and accept an Elastic IP — the answer when a client's firewall must allow specific addresses.
Preserve the client's source IP all the way to the target.
Serve as the entry point for a **PrivateLink** endpoint service.

blocks.x: A Gateway Load Balancer is not for application traffic. It exists to route packets transparently through third-party appliances — firewalls, intrusion detection, deep packet inspection — and back.

checks.q: Clients must connect to a fixed set of IP addresses that their firewalls allow. Which load balancer?

o.t: Any of them — all support static IPs

checks.x: Only the NLB gives a static IP per Availability Zone and accepts an Elastic IP. An ALB is reached by DNS name and its addresses change.

checks.q: Requests for /api must go to one target group and /images to another. Which load balancer?
checks.x: Path-based routing is a layer 7 feature and only the ALB can read the URL. An NLB works at layer 4 and sees ports, not paths.

checks.q: A game server uses UDP. Which load balancer supports it?

o.t: Neither — UDP cannot be load balanced on AWS

checks.x: The NLB is the only one that handles UDP, because it works at the transport layer. ALBs are HTTP and HTTPS only.

checks.q: Targets behind an ALB see the load balancer's IP address rather than the client's. How do they get the real client address?

o.t: From the target group's health check

checks.x: An ALB terminates the connection and opens a new one to the target, so it records the original address in X-Forwarded-For. An NLB does not need this because it preserves the source IP directly.

modules.goal: Explain how a load balancer decides a target is healthy and how it keeps a session in place.

blocks.x: Health checks

The load balancer polls each target on a port and path. A target failing the threshold stops receiving traffic; it is not terminated — that is Auto Scaling's job, if you tell it to use ELB health checks.

x: Health check fails
Target marked unhealthy
Traffic stops going to it
ASG replaces it — if it uses ELB health checks
blocks.cap: Without that last link, a broken-but-running instance stays in the group forever.

blocks.x: An Auto Scaling group defaults to **EC2 health checks**, which only notice a stopped instance. Set the health check type to **ELB** so an instance that is running but failing its health check is replaced.
Sticky sessions

x: Stickiness sends one client back to the same target, using a cookie.
The **AWSALB** cookie is generated by the load balancer; an application cookie may be used instead.
It causes uneven load, and it is a workaround — the better answer is to move session state out to **ElastiCache** or **DynamoDB**.
NLB stickiness is per source IP, not per cookie.

blocks.x: Cross-zone load balancing

head: Application Load Balancer
Network Load Balancer
rows: **On**, and it cannot be turned off
Each zone takes an equal share regardless of target count

blocks.x: With cross-zone off, each Availability Zone gets an equal share of traffic regardless of how many targets are in it. Two instances in one zone and eight in another means the two carry half the load.
TLS and connection handling

x: Certificates come from **ACM**, free for use with a load balancer, and renew automatically.
**SNI** lets one load balancer serve many certificates for many hostnames.
**Connection draining** — deregistration delay — lets in-flight requests finish before a target is removed. Default 300 seconds, tunable from 0 to 3600.

checks.q: An instance is running but its application has crashed, and Auto Scaling never replaces it. What is misconfigured?

o.t: The group is using EC2 health checks instead of ELB health checks
The load balancer has no listener
The instance has no Elastic IP

checks.x: EC2 health checks only report whether the instance itself is running. Switching the group to ELB health checks means a target failing the load balancer's check is treated as unhealthy and replaced.

checks.q: Users are being logged out when their requests land on different servers. What is the quickest fix, and what is the better one?

o.t: Increase the deregistration delay now; shorten it later
Enable sticky sessions now; move session state to ElastiCache or DynamoDB properly
Enable cross-zone load balancing now; add an Elastic IP later
Disable health checks now; add more instances later

checks.x: Stickiness pins a client to one target and solves the symptom immediately, at the cost of uneven load. Externalising session state removes the requirement altogether, which is why it is the architecturally correct answer.

checks.q: Cross-zone load balancing is disabled on an NLB. Zone A has two targets and zone B has eight. How is traffic distributed?

o.t: Only to zone B, which has more capacity
Half to each zone, so each target in zone A receives four times as much
Round robin weighted by instance size

checks.x: Without cross-zone balancing, traffic is split evenly between zones first and only then among the targets inside each zone. That is why an uneven target count becomes an uneven load.

checks.q: What does the deregistration delay control?

o.t: How long a sticky session lasts
How long a TLS certificate is cached
How long in-flight requests may finish before a target is removed

checks.x: Also called connection draining, it stops the load balancer cutting off requests mid-flight when an instance is being taken out of service. The default is 300 seconds.

modules.goal: Set minimum, desired and maximum correctly, and say what replaces an unhealthy instance.

blocks.x: An **Auto Scaling group** keeps a chosen number of instances running, launching and terminating them to match. It gives you elasticity *and* self-healing, and the exam cares about both.

head: Setting
Meaning
rows: Never go below this, even with no traffic
What the group aims for right now — scaling policies move this number
Never go above this, however busy it gets
What a new instance looks like: AMI, type, security groups, user data, role

blocks.x: An Auto Scaling group spanning **multiple Availability Zones** is what makes an architecture survive losing a zone. A group in one zone is a single point of failure, no matter how many instances it holds.
Self-healing

x: An instance failing its health check is terminated and replaced.
With **ELB health checks** the group also replaces instances whose application is broken.
A **health check grace period** stops the group killing an instance before it has finished booting — too short a grace period causes an endless replace loop.
**Lifecycle hooks** pause an instance as it launches or terminates, so you can install something or drain it cleanly.

blocks.x: Launch templates
Launch configurations are legacy and immutable. **Launch templates** are versioned, support mixed instance types and Spot, and are the expected answer.
An instance stuck in a launch-terminate loop usually has a health check grace period that is shorter than its boot time, or a user data script that fails. The fix is not a larger instance.

checks.q: What makes an Auto Scaling group survive the loss of an Availability Zone?

o.t: Configuring it across subnets in several Availability Zones
Attaching Elastic IPs to its instances

checks.x: Spanning zones is the point: if one zone fails the group launches replacements in the others. A larger maximum in a single zone does not help when that zone is the thing that failed.

checks.q: New instances are terminated shortly after launching, before the application finishes starting. What should be adjusted?
checks.x: The grace period tells the group how long to wait before health checks count. When it is shorter than the boot time, every new instance is judged unhealthy and replaced, producing a loop.

checks.q: Which should be used to define what a new instance looks like?
checks.x: Launch templates are versioned and support mixed instance types and purchase options. Launch configurations are the legacy, immutable predecessor and are no longer the expected answer.

checks.q: You need to run a script on an instance before it is removed from the group. What provides the pause?
checks.x: A lifecycle hook holds an instance in a wait state as it launches or terminates, giving you time to act. The deregistration delay only drains connections at the load balancer.

modules.goal: Choose target tracking, step, simple or scheduled scaling from the trigger described.

head: Policy
How it decides
Reach for it when
rows: Keep a metric at a value, like average CPU at 50%
The default answer — simplest and usually right
Add more instances the further the alarm is breached
The response should be proportional to how bad it is
One action per alarm, then wait for a cooldown
A known pattern — market open, a sale, month end
A recurring daily or weekly shape, scaled before it arrives

blocks.x: "Keep average CPU around X" is target tracking. "Every weekday at 9 a.m." is scheduled scaling. "Scale ahead of the pattern we see every day" is predictive.
Useful metrics

x: `ASGAverageCPUUtilization` — the usual starting point.
`ALBRequestCountPerTarget` — better for web tiers, because requests are the load, not CPU.
`ASGAverageNetworkIn` and `NetworkOut` for bandwidth-bound work.
A **custom metric** such as queue depth — the standard answer for scaling workers on an SQS queue.

blocks.x: Scaling on a queue

x: Messages pile up in SQS
ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible rises
CloudWatch alarm
ASG adds workers
Backlog drains
blocks.cap: Scale on backlog per instance, not CPU — a worker waiting on I/O looks idle.

blocks.x: Cooldowns and warm-up
A **cooldown** stops the group reacting again before the last change has taken effect. Target tracking uses an **instance warm-up** instead, so instances still booting are not counted in the metric.
Scaling a queue-consuming fleet on CPU is a classic wrong answer. Workers blocked on I/O show low CPU while the backlog grows — scale on the number of messages instead.

checks.q: A web tier should keep average CPU near 60%. Which scaling policy?
checks.x: Target tracking takes a metric and a target value and manages the rest. Naming a value to hold is the phrasing that points straight at it.

checks.q: Traffic rises every weekday at 08:00 and the fleet is always a few minutes behind. What addresses it most directly?

o.t: Scheduled scaling that adds capacity before 08:00

checks.x: A known clock-time pattern is what scheduled scaling exists for: capacity is in place before the load arrives rather than reacting after it. Predictive scaling is the automatic version of the same idea.

checks.q: Workers consume an SQS queue. Their CPU stays low while the backlog grows. What should the group scale on?

o.t: The number of visible messages in the queue

checks.x: The backlog is the real measure of work waiting. Workers blocked on I/O look idle by CPU, so a CPU-based policy never scales out while the queue keeps growing.

checks.q: What does an instance warm-up setting do for a target tracking policy?

o.t: Keeps a minimum number of instances running
Excludes instances that are still starting from the metric

checks.x: Instances that are still booting would otherwise drag the average down and trigger more scaling. The warm-up period leaves them out of the calculation until they are serving.

Default
Why it matters

Too short and instances are killed before they boot
In-flight requests finish before a target leaves

recap.x: Multi-AZ Auto Scaling behind a load balancer is the shape of nearly every highly available answer on this exam. One zone, or no load balancer, is what makes an option wrong.

head: The question says
Policy
rows: Keep this metric at this value
Learn the daily pattern and act ahead of it

items: ASG with ELB health checks terminates it

recap.x: Recurring distractors: an ALB where a static IP is required; scaling a queue fleet on CPU; leaving the health check type on EC2; a single-AZ Auto Scaling group described as highly available; and sticky sessions offered as a scaling improvement.

final.q: A partner's firewall can only allow traffic to specific IP addresses, and the workload is plain TCP. Which load balancer meets this?

o.t: A Network Load Balancer, which provides a static IP per Availability Zone
o.w: Correct — the NLB is the only load balancer that offers static addressing, including Elastic IPs.
A Gateway Load Balancer routes traffic to inspection appliances and is not the entry point for an application.

o.t: An Application Load Balancer with an Elastic IP attached
o.w: An ALB cannot be given an Elastic IP at all.

o.t: An Application Load Balancer with a Route 53 alias
o.w: An alias record still resolves to changing ALB addresses, which a firewall allow-list cannot pin.

final.x: "The client firewall must allow specific IPs" is the strongest NLB signal on the exam. ALBs are addressed by name, and their addresses change.

final.q: Instances in an Auto Scaling group keep running after their application process dies, and users see errors. What change fixes this?

o.w: More instances means more broken ones too; nothing detects the failure.

o.t: Set the group's health check type to ELB
o.w: Correct — with ELB health checks the group treats a failing load balancer check as an unhealthy instance and replaces it.
Cross-zone balancing changes distribution, not health detection.
Draining affects how targets leave, not whether they are found unhealthy.

final.x: EC2 health checks only see whether the virtual machine is running. Pointing the group at the load balancer's health check is what makes the architecture self-healing at the application level.

final.q: A fleet of workers pulls jobs from an SQS queue. During busy periods the queue grows for hours while CPU stays near 15%. How should the group scale?

o.t: On the count of healthy hosts
o.w: Healthy host count is an output of scaling, not an input to it.

o.t: On average CPU utilisation with a lower target
o.w: Lowering a CPU target still measures the wrong thing; I/O-bound workers never reach it.

o.t: On a custom metric derived from the number of messages waiting in the queue
o.w: Correct — the backlog is the work waiting, and scaling on it adds workers exactly when jobs are queued.
Network volume does not track job count for small messages with long processing times.

final.x: Queue depth, ideally as a backlog-per-instance figure, is the standard answer for worker fleets. CPU-based scaling fails precisely because a worker waiting on I/O looks idle.

final.q: A single domain serves a web application at /shop and an API at /api, each running on its own fleet. What routes them?

o.t: Two Elastic IPs and a Route 53 failover record
o.w: Failover records choose between endpoints for availability, not by URL path.

o.t: A Network Load Balancer with two listeners
o.w: An NLB sees ports and addresses, never the request path.

o.t: A Gateway Load Balancer with two appliance groups
o.w: Gateway Load Balancers pass packets to inspection appliances and cannot route on paths.

o.t: An Application Load Balancer with path-based rules to two target groups
o.w: Correct — reading the URL path is a layer 7 capability, and rules can send each path to its own target group.

final.x: Path-based routing is the defining ALB feature, alongside host-based rules, header matching and Lambda targets. Anything that has to read HTTP is an ALB question.

final.q: Deployments cut off user requests mid-flight when instances are taken out of service. What setting addresses this?

o.t: The deregistration delay, also known as connection draining
o.w: Correct — it keeps a departing target alive long enough to finish requests already in progress.
Warm-up concerns instances arriving, not leaving.
The health check interval changes how quickly failures are noticed, not how targets are removed.
Stickiness routes a client consistently; it does not protect in-flight requests during removal.

final.x: Connection draining exists for exactly this: the target stops receiving new requests but keeps serving existing ones for up to the configured delay, which defaults to 300 seconds.

final.q: Traffic to a retail site climbs sharply at 19:00 every evening and the fleet is always several minutes behind demand. Which approach removes the lag?

o.t: Moving to an NLB for faster routing
o.w: Changing load balancer type does nothing about insufficient capacity.

o.t: Scheduled scaling that raises desired capacity shortly before 19:00
o.w: Correct — capacity is added ahead of a known clock-time pattern rather than reacting after the load arrives.
Stickiness does not reduce total load; it only pins clients to targets.

o.t: A shorter cooldown on a simple scaling policy
o.w: Reacting faster still means reacting after users are already waiting.

final.x: A repeating clock-time pattern is scheduled scaling's exact use case; predictive scaling automates the same idea from history. Reactive policies always trail a sharp ramp.

final.q: An NLB has cross-zone load balancing disabled. One Availability Zone holds two targets and another holds eight. What is the consequence?

o.t: Traffic is spread evenly across all ten targets
o.w: Even per-target distribution is what enabling cross-zone balancing would achieve.

o.t: Health checks fail in the smaller zone
o.w: Uneven distribution does not itself cause health check failures, though overload eventually might.

o.t: Each zone receives half the traffic, so the two targets carry four times the per-target load
o.w: Correct — traffic is divided between zones first, and only then among the targets inside each zone.

o.t: The zone with two targets is removed from service
o.w: Zones are not removed for having fewer targets.

final.x: This is why NLB target counts should be balanced per zone, or cross-zone enabled — with the caveat that enabling it on an NLB adds inter-AZ data transfer charges.

final.q: An Auto Scaling group must run a configuration script and register an instance with an external system before it starts receiving traffic. What provides the pause?

o.w: Cooldowns govern how soon another scaling action may occur, not what happens to one instance.
Scheduled actions change capacity at a time; they do not pause an individual launch.
Deregistration delay applies when an instance leaves, not when it joins.

o.t: A lifecycle hook on instance launch
o.w: Correct — the hook holds the instance in a pending wait state until the work completes or the timeout expires.

final.x: Lifecycle hooks exist on both launch and terminate, which makes them the answer for install-before-serving and drain-before-terminate requirements alike.

final.q: An application must authenticate users with an OIDC identity provider before any request reaches the backend, with no authentication code in the application. What supports this?

o.t: An Application Load Balancer configured to authenticate with OIDC or Cognito
o.w: Correct — the ALB can complete the authentication flow itself and pass user claims to the target.

o.t: A Gateway Load Balancer with an identity appliance
o.w: Gateway Load Balancers forward packets to appliances and do not perform user authentication.
Route 53 resolves names and has no notion of a user session.

o.t: A Network Load Balancer with TLS termination
o.w: An NLB works at layer 4 and cannot participate in an HTTP authentication flow.

final.x: Built-in authentication is an ALB feature that removes login handling from the application entirely: unauthenticated requests are redirected to the provider and only authenticated ones reach the target group.

final.q: A new target tracking policy keeps adding instances during a scale-out, overshooting the required capacity. Which setting most directly reduces the overshoot?

o.t: A shorter health check grace period
o.w: A shorter grace period risks terminating healthy instances mid-boot.

o.t: An instance warm-up period, so instances that are still starting are excluded from the metric
o.w: Correct — booting instances contribute no work but count in the average, which drags the metric down and triggers further scaling.
Stickiness has no effect on how the scaling metric is calculated.
A larger maximum permits more overshoot rather than preventing it.

final.x: Overshoot in target tracking usually comes from counting instances that are not yet serving. The warm-up period leaves them out until they are ready, which stabilises the loop.

modules.nm: RDS, and what AWS manages for you
modules.goal: Say what RDS takes over from you, and what it refuses to give you.

blocks.x: **RDS** runs a relational database engine for you — MySQL, PostgreSQL, MariaDB, Oracle, SQL Server, and Aurora. You get the database; AWS keeps the machine.

items: Provisioning and patching the operating system
Storage that grows on its own
Anything that needs an OS-level agent

blocks.x: "We need SSH access to the database server" rules RDS out. That requirement means EC2, or **RDS Custom** for Oracle and SQL Server, which deliberately gives back host access.
Backups

head: Automated backups
Manual snapshots
rows: Daily, plus transaction logs every 5 minutes
Any point in time within the window
Yes, unless a final snapshot is taken

blocks.x: Storage autoscaling
RDS can grow its storage automatically when free space runs low, up to a maximum you set. It is the answer when an application's data growth is unpredictable — storage never shrinks back.
A restore always creates a **new database instance with a new endpoint**. Any answer that implies restoring "in place" over the existing instance is wrong.

checks.q: A workload needs an agent installed on the database host's operating system. What does that rule out?

o.t: Standard RDS, because it gives no OS access

checks.x: RDS is a managed service and never grants host access. The requirement points at running the engine on EC2, or at RDS Custom where AWS deliberately hands back operating system control.

checks.q: How far back can RDS point-in-time recovery reach by default configuration limits?

o.t: Up to 35 days, depending on the retention period set
Only to the most recent daily backup

checks.x: Automated backups retain between 1 and 35 days, and transaction logs are captured every five minutes, so any moment inside the window can be restored. Manual snapshots persist indefinitely but restore only to their own point in time.

checks.q: What happens when you restore an RDS backup?

o.t: The existing instance is overwritten in place
A new database instance is created with a new endpoint
The data is merged into the running instance

checks.x: Restores always produce a new instance, which means the application's connection string has to be repointed. That is why answers claiming an in-place restore are wrong.

checks.q: An application's data volume is unpredictable and the database keeps running out of space. What addresses it?

o.t: Enable RDS storage autoscaling with a maximum threshold

checks.x: Storage autoscaling grows the volume when free space drops below a threshold, up to a limit you set. Replicas and Multi-AZ address reads and availability, not capacity.

modules.goal: Tell availability apart from scale, and pick the right one for a stated requirement.

blocks.x: These two are confused constantly, and the exam relies on it. One is for **surviving failure**; the other is for **serving more reads**.

head: Multi-AZ
Read replicas
rows: Same AZ, another AZ, or **another region**

blocks.x: "Reporting queries are slowing the production database" → a read replica. "The database must survive an Availability Zone failure" → Multi-AZ. A question can want both, and the answer then uses both.
What failover actually does

x: The primary fails
RDS promotes the standby
The DNS endpoint now points at it
The application reconnects
blocks.cap: The endpoint name does not change, which is why applications need only reconnect.

blocks.x: Consistency

x: Multi-AZ replication is synchronous, so the standby is always current.
Read replica replication is asynchronous, so a read may return slightly **stale data** — the reason they are unsuitable for anything requiring read-after-write consistency.
A cross-region read replica also serves disaster recovery and cuts read latency for a distant region.

blocks.x: Promoting a read replica breaks replication permanently and turns it into an independent database. It is a disaster recovery action, not a routine one.

checks.q: A nightly analytics job is slowing down the production database. What is the standard fix?

o.t: Point the job at a read replica

checks.x: Read replicas exist to take read load off the primary. Multi-AZ adds a standby that serves no traffic at all, so it would not help this at all.

checks.q: Which statement about Multi-AZ is correct?

o.t: The standby is in the same Availability Zone
Replication is synchronous and the standby serves no traffic
Replication is asynchronous and the standby can be read
You can have up to five standbys

checks.x: Multi-AZ is purely about availability: writes are committed to both instances synchronously, and the standby stays idle until a failover promotes it.

checks.q: An application must always read data it has just written. What rules out a read replica for those reads?

o.t: Replication is asynchronous, so a replica can return stale data
Replicas cannot be in another Availability Zone

checks.x: Replication lag means a write may not have reached the replica yet. Reads that must be immediately consistent have to go to the primary.

checks.q: What happens when a read replica is promoted?

o.t: It is deleted after the promotion
It keeps replicating but also accepts writes
It becomes an independent database and replication stops permanently

checks.x: Promotion is one-way: the replica stops following the source and becomes a standalone database. That makes it a recovery step rather than something used routinely.

modules.goal: Name what Aurora changes about storage and endpoints, and when to use its variants.

blocks.x: **Aurora** is an AWS-built engine compatible with MySQL and PostgreSQL. What is different is underneath: a shared, distributed storage layer rather than a disk per instance.

x: Storage is replicated **six ways across three Availability Zones**, and grows automatically up to 128 TB.
Up to **15 read replicas**, all reading the same storage, so replica lag is very low.

o.w: Removing the health check makes the record eligible again rather than draining it.

o.w: Switching the policy discards the split entirely and changes behaviour unpredictably.

final.q: A team plans to repoint a production record to a new load balancer next Tuesday and needs the change to take effect quickly. What should they do this week?

o.w: A higher TTL makes the change propagate more slowly, which is the opposite of the goal.

o.w: Record type does not control propagation speed.

Simple routing returns values without steering by anything.
Correct — latency routing uses measured latency between the user's network and each region.
Geolocation enforces a mapping by location and ignores measured speed.

o.w: Publishing private addresses in a public zone exposes internal naming to anyone who queries it.

o.w: A CNAME chain does not restrict who can resolve the name.

o.w: Correct — a private hosted zone answers only for the VPCs it is associated with.

o.t: A Route 53 Resolver inbound endpoint in the VPC
o.w: Correct — the inbound endpoint gives on-premises resolvers IP addresses in the VPC to forward queries to.

o.t: A NAT gateway for DNS traffic
o.w: A NAT gateway carries traffic but does not answer DNS queries for a private zone.

o.t: A Route 53 Resolver outbound endpoint in the VPC
o.w: The outbound endpoint is for the opposite direction, when VPC resources query on-premises DNS.

o.t: A public hosted zone mirroring the names
o.w: Mirroring internal names publicly defeats the purpose of a private zone.

o.t: An A record with the current address
o.w: A hard-coded address breaks the next time the provider changes it.

o.t: A CNAME record pointing at the provider's hostname
o.w: Correct — a CNAME follows the provider's own DNS, so address changes need no action from you.

o.t: A multivalue record listing known addresses
o.w: Listing addresses manually has the same staleness problem, multiplied.

o.t: An alias record pointing at the provider's hostname
o.w: Alias records can only target a defined set of AWS resources, not external names.

Up to 5 TB, and anything over 5 GB must use multipart upload
Eleven nines, across at least three Availability Zones
**Strong read-after-write** for new objects, overwrites and deletes

What S3 is not

x: Not a file system. It has no partial writes and no rename — a rename is a copy plus a delete.
Not block storage — you cannot mount it as a disk and boot from it.
Not free to list: listing millions of keys costs requests and time, which is why prefixes matter.
Client PUT
Object stored across three or more Availability Zones
GET returns it immediately

checks.q: What does a slash in an object key represent?

o.t: The boundary between bucket and region
A real directory created in the bucket
An ordinary character that listings treat as a folder boundary

The bucket has no CORS configuration

A VPC gateway endpoint for S3
A presigned URL for each object

Objects present before versioning was enabled have a version id of `null`.
**MFA Delete** requires a multi-factor code to delete a version or suspend versioning — and it can only be enabled by the **bucket owner using the root account**.

Object Lock

Effect

**Nobody**, including the root user, can delete before the retention expires

o.t: A delete marker is added and the object is hidden but recoverable
The object and all its versions are permanently removed

Versioning was enabled on the destination

The objects are in a different storage class

Both buckets are in the same region
Versioning is enabled on both the source and destination buckets

**Expiration actions** delete objects, old versions, or incomplete multipart uploads.

blocks.x: "We must be able to audit every use of the key" or "control who can decrypt" means **SSE-KMS**, because KMS logs each call to CloudTrail and enforces a key policy.

Every object read or written with SSE-KMS calls KMS, which counts against KMS request quotas and costs money. **S3 Bucket Keys** cut those calls dramatically for high-volume buckets — the standard answer when SSE-KMS causes throttling or an unexpected KMS bill.

x: Buckets encrypt with SSE-S3 by default; default encryption can be set to a KMS key instead.
To *force* a particular method, use a **bucket policy that denies PutObject** unless the request carries the right `x-amz-server-side-encryption` header.
Enabling default encryption does not re-encrypt objects that are already there.

blocks.x: With SSE-C the key travels in the request, so S3 refuses the call over plain HTTP. An option that uses SSE-C over HTTP is wrong on that alone.

checks.x: A bucket key is derived once and reused for many objects, which cuts KMS requests sharply. Switching to SSE-C moves key handling to the client rather than solving the throttling properly.

checks.x: Default encryption silently encrypts anything that arrives unencrypted, which is not the same as rejecting it. A deny policy conditioned on the encryption header is what actually enforces the rule.

o.t: Because the object is stored in one Availability Zone
S3 requires HTTPS for all requests
Because KMS is called on every request
The encryption key is sent in the request itself

checks.x: With SSE-C you provide the key on every call, so sending it over an unencrypted connection would expose it. S3 rejects such requests outright.

blocks.x: **SQS** is a queue. Producers write messages, consumers read and then delete them. Nothing is pushed — a consumer **polls**. The point is that producer and consumer no longer have to be available at the same moment or run at the same speed.

x: Consumer receives a message
It becomes invisible to others
Consumer finishes and deletes it
If not deleted in time, it reappears

Too **long** and a failed consumer's message is stuck waiting before anyone can retry it.

A **subscription filter policy** means a subscriber only receives messages matching attributes it cares about. That is cheaper and simpler than every consumer receiving everything and discarding most of it.

final.q: An application queries a DynamoDB table by customer id, and a new report must find orders by status. The table is in production with millions of items. What should be added?

o.t: A scheduled scan writing results to S3
o.w: Scanning millions of items repeatedly is expensive and slow, which indexes exist to avoid.

o.t: A global secondary index on status
o.w: Correct — a GSI can use a different partition key and can be added to an existing table.
DAX caches reads; it does not create a new access pattern.

o.t: A local secondary index on status
o.w: Local secondary indexes must be created with the table and keep the original partition key.

final.x: New access patterns on an existing table are global secondary indexes. The LSI restriction — same partition key, defined at creation — is what makes it the wrong answer here.

final.q: A Lambda function was moved into private subnets to reach an RDS database. It now succeeds against the database but every call to an external payment API times out. What is required?

o.t: An internet gateway attached directly to the private subnets
o.w: Attaching an internet gateway to a subnet does not make it private, and private subnets route through NAT by design.

o.t: RDS Proxy in front of the database
o.w: RDS Proxy addresses connection pooling, not outbound internet access.

o.t: A NAT gateway in a public subnet with a route from the function's subnets
o.w: Correct — a VPC-attached function has no internet path until one is provided, and a NAT gateway is that path.
A longer timeout waits longer for a connection that can never be established.

final.x: This is the standard trade-off of putting Lambda in a VPC: private resources become reachable and the internet does not, until a NAT gateway or VPC endpoint restores the path you need.

final.q: A public API must let each customer make no more than 100 requests per second, with a monthly quota per customer. What provides this?

o.t: Reserved concurrency on the backing Lambda function
o.w: Reserved concurrency caps the whole function, not individual customers.

o.t: AWS WAF rate-based rules on the stage
o.w: WAF rate rules work on IP addresses rather than identified customers.

o.t: CloudFront caching in front of the API
o.w: Caching reduces backend load but enforces no per-customer limit.

o.t: API Gateway usage plans with API keys, throttling and quotas
o.w: Correct — usage plans attach per-key rate, burst and quota limits, which is exactly per-customer metering.

final.x: Per-client limits and quotas are what usage plans exist for. WAF rate limiting is the answer to abusive traffic by address, which is a different question.

final.q: A gaming table sees uneven performance: one partition key value receives most of the traffic. What is the correct remedy?

o.t: Redesign the partition key to spread requests, for example by adding a suffix
o.w: Correct — throughput is distributed by partition key, so an even key distribution is the only real fix.

o.t: Increase the read capacity units on the table
o.w: More capacity on a table with one hot key still throttles that key.
An index adds an access pattern; it does not rebalance the base table's traffic.

o.t: Switch from on-demand to provisioned capacity
o.w: Capacity mode does not change how requests map to partitions.

final.x: Hot partitions come from key design. Adding a computed suffix, or choosing a higher-cardinality attribute, is what spreads the load across partitions.

final.q: An API's p99 latency spikes whenever traffic arrives after a quiet period, and the business requires consistent response times during business hours. What should be configured?

o.t: A smaller memory allocation to speed initialisation
o.w: Less memory means less CPU and slower initialisation, making the problem worse.

o.t: Provisioned concurrency, optionally scheduled for business hours
o.w: Correct — provisioned concurrency keeps environments initialised so requests avoid the cold start entirely.

o.t: Reserved concurrency set to the expected peak
o.w: Reserved concurrency limits how many copies may run; it does not pre-warm anything.
Timeout governs how long a function may run, not how quickly it starts.

final.x: Cold starts are an initialisation cost paid by the first request into a new environment. Provisioned concurrency pays it in advance, and Application Auto Scaling can schedule it around known traffic.

final.q: A mobile application authenticates users and must then upload photographs directly to S3 without routing the files through a backend. What combination is correct?

o.t: An IAM user created for each mobile device
o.w: Creating an IAM user per device does not scale and leaves long-lived credentials on phones.

o.t: API Gateway with a Lambda proxy that forwards the file
o.w: Routing large files through Lambda is exactly what the requirement avoids.

o.t: A Cognito user pool for sign-in and an identity pool to obtain temporary AWS credentials
o.w: Correct — the user pool authenticates and the identity pool exchanges that identity for scoped STS credentials.

o.t: A Cognito user pool alone, with the app using its JWT to call S3
o.w: S3 does not accept a Cognito JWT; it requires AWS credentials.

final.x: The two Cognito halves do different jobs: authentication in the user pool, AWS authorisation in the identity pool. Direct-to-S3 uploads need the second one.

final.q: An S3 event triggers a Lambda function asynchronously. Some events fail every time due to malformed files, and the team needs to inspect them. What should be configured?

o.w: Zero reserved concurrency would stop the function entirely.
S3 event notifications to Lambda are asynchronous; this is not configurable.

o.t: A longer timeout on the function
o.w: A longer timeout does not help an event that fails because of its content.

o.t: An on-failure destination or dead-letter queue for the function
o.w: Correct — after Lambda's two automatic retries, the event is delivered there for inspection instead of being lost.

final.x: Asynchronous invocations retry twice and then need somewhere to go. Failure destinations and dead-letter queues are how bad events are captured rather than silently discarded.

final.q: A global application must accept writes in three regions with low latency in each, on a key-value data model. What fits?

o.w: Correct — Global Tables provide multi-region, multi-active replication built into the service.
DynamoDB has no separate cross-region read replica feature of that kind.
Aurora is relational and its global database has a single writable region.

o.t: DynamoDB Streams replicating with custom Lambda code
o.w: Hand-built replication with Streams is possible but reimplements a managed feature badly.

final.x: Writes accepted in several regions on a key-value model is Global Tables' exact description. Aurora Global Database is the relational analogue but with one primary region for writes.

final.q: An internal API must be reachable only from inside the company's VPCs and never from the internet. How should it be exposed?

o.t: A regional API protected by a resource policy listing office IPs
o.w: An IP allow-list still leaves the API exposed on the internet.

o.t: A private API Gateway endpoint accessed through an interface VPC endpoint
o.w: Correct — a private endpoint type has no public DNS path and is reached only through PrivateLink.

o.t: An edge-optimised API behind CloudFront with geo restriction
o.w: Geo restriction filters by country and does not make the API private.

o.t: A public API with a usage plan and API keys
o.w: API keys identify callers but do not restrict network reachability.

final.x: Private endpoint type plus an interface VPC endpoint is the supported way to keep an API entirely off the internet, which is stronger than any address-based restriction.

blocks.x: AWS offers a database per data shape rather than one database for everything. Exam questions in this area are pure pattern matching: find the sentence that names the shape.

Category
Service

blocks.x: The phrases that give it away: **"relationships"** or "friends of friends" means Neptune; **"time series"** or "sensor readings over time" means Timestream; **"complex analytical queries"** means Redshift.
Managed or not

Which access pattern dominates?
What are the availability and scale needs?

checks.q: An application must answer questions like "which customers are connected to this customer through two or fewer relationships". Which database?
checks.x: Traversing relationships is a graph query, which is what Neptune is built for. Expressing the same thing in a key-value or relational model requires expensive repeated joins.

checks.q: Millions of sensor readings arrive with a timestamp and must be queried over time windows. Which database?
checks.x: Timestream is purpose-built for time series: it stores recent and historical data in different tiers and has time-window functions built in.

checks.q: When is running a database engine on EC2 the right answer?

o.t: When operating system access or an unsupported engine version is required

checks.x: Managed services are preferred unless something specific rules them out, and host access or an unsupported engine is that something. Availability and cost usually argue for the managed option.

checks.q: A workload runs complex analytical queries aggregating billions of rows. Which service fits?
checks.x: Redshift is a columnar data warehouse built for large aggregations. Key-value and wide-column stores are optimised for point lookups, not for scanning and summarising whole datasets.

modules.goal: Justify choosing DynamoDB or a relational database for a stated access pattern.

items: Scales up, and out for reads with replicas
Writes scale by making the instance bigger
Known access patterns, looked up by key
Single-digit millisecond latency at any scale
No joins; you design the keys around the queries

blocks.x: The deciding question is whether the **access patterns are known in advance**. If they are, DynamoDB scales further and costs less to operate. If the application needs ad-hoc queries and joins, use a relational database.
Where each one hurts

head: Problem
Relational
DynamoDB
rows: Needs a new index, or a redesign
Awkward — export to S3 and use Athena

blocks.x: Aurora, when relational is right

x: **Aurora Serverless v2** for intermittent or unpredictable load.
**Aurora Global Database** for cross-region recovery in about a minute.
**Reader endpoint** for spreading read traffic across up to fifteen replicas.
Standard **RDS** when the engine is Oracle or SQL Server, or when Aurora's compatibility is not needed.

blocks.x: "Migrate a relational application to DynamoDB to make it scale" is usually wrong unless the question says the access patterns are simple and known. A join-heavy application rewritten onto a key-value store is a rewrite, not a migration.

checks.q: A shopping cart is always read and written by cart id, and write volume grows unpredictably. Which database fits best?
checks.x: A single known access pattern by key with unbounded write growth is exactly DynamoDB's profile, and it scales writes horizontally with no capacity planning.

checks.q: An analytics team needs to run ad-hoc joins across ten tables that change weekly. Which database?

o.t: A relational database such as Aurora

checks.x: Ad-hoc joins across changing tables are what SQL and a relational engine are for. In a key-value store each new pattern needs a new index or a redesign.

checks.q: Which statement about scaling writes is correct?

o.t: DynamoDB scales writes only with provisioned capacity
DynamoDB scales writes horizontally; a relational database usually scales writes by growing the instance
Both scale writes horizontally by default

checks.x: Relational read replicas take read load but all writes still go to one primary. DynamoDB distributes writes across partitions, which is why it is chosen for very high write volume.

checks.q: A workload is relational but idle for most of the day with unpredictable bursts. Which option fits?

o.t: A provisioned RDS instance sized for the peak

checks.x: Serverless v2 scales capacity with demand, so idle periods are cheap and bursts are absorbed without a redesign. Keeping a peak-sized instance running pays for capacity that is mostly unused.

modules.goal: Recognise the one-line description of DocumentDB, Keyspaces, Neptune and Timestream.

Compatible with
Reach for it when
