An existing Cassandra workload, or a wide-column model, without running the cluster
Relationships are the query: social graphs, fraud rings, recommendations, knowledge graphs
Measurements arriving with timestamps, queried over windows
Analytical queries over very large datasets

blocks.x: Compatibility is the signal. MongoDB means DocumentDB; Cassandra means Keyspaces. Neither is a general-purpose answer — they exist so an existing application does not have to be rewritten.
Timestream's shape

Timestream keeps recent data in a **memory store** for fast queries and moves older data to a cheaper **magnetic store** on a schedule you set, which is why it is far cheaper than a relational database for the same data.
Redshift, briefly

x: Columnar storage with massively parallel processing across nodes.
**Concurrency scaling** adds capacity for bursts of queries.
**Redshift Spectrum** queries data that is still in S3, without loading it.
It is a warehouse, not a transactional database — it is the wrong answer for high-volume single-row writes.

blocks.x: Redshift is for analytics, not for an application's live transactions. An option that puts an online transaction workload on Redshift is wrong however well the scale seems to match.

checks.q: An existing MongoDB application must move to a managed service with minimal code change. Which service?
checks.x: DocumentDB is MongoDB compatible, so drivers and queries carry over. DynamoDB has a different API entirely and would require the data access layer to be rewritten.

checks.q: A team runs Apache Cassandra on EC2 and wants the same CQL interface without managing nodes. Which service?
checks.x: Keyspaces is Cassandra compatible and serverless, so existing CQL applications connect with little change and there is no cluster to operate.

checks.q: How does Timestream keep costs low for long retention?

o.t: It stores only aggregates, not raw readings
It compresses everything into a single file
Recent data sits in a memory store and older data moves to a cheaper magnetic store
It deletes data older than 30 days

checks.x: The tiered storage model means fast queries over recent data and cheap storage for history, with the transition governed by a retention policy you configure.

checks.q: Why is Redshift the wrong choice for an application's live transactional writes?

o.t: It cannot be accessed from a VPC
It cannot store more than a terabyte
It is a columnar analytical warehouse, not a transactional database

checks.x: Columnar storage and parallel scans make aggregation fast but single-row inserts and updates slow. Transactional workloads belong in RDS, Aurora or DynamoDB.

Why

blocks.x: A cache is never the answer when the question forbids application changes, and a warehouse is never the answer for live transactions. Those two constraints eliminate options quickly.

checks.q: A read-heavy product page hits a relational database hard, and the team may change the application. What is the usual addition?

o.t: ElastiCache in front of the database

checks.x: Caching frequently read data removes most of the repeated queries. It requires application changes, which the question explicitly permits.

checks.q: Which pairing gives microsecond reads on a key-value workload with almost no code change?

o.t: Keyspaces with a global secondary index

checks.x: DAX speaks the DynamoDB API, so only the endpoint changes. ElastiCache would require the application to implement its own cache logic.

checks.q: Data already sits in S3 and analysts want SQL over it without loading it anywhere. What fits?

o.t: Amazon Redshift with a full load

checks.x: Athena queries data in place in S3 and charges per data scanned, which avoids any loading step or cluster to run.

checks.q: Two options both match the data shape. What usually decides between them on this exam?

o.t: Which one has a shorter name
Which one was released more recently
Which one supports the most regions
Which one has lower operational overhead or scales further

checks.x: The exam consistently favours the more managed option and the one that scales to the stated requirement, unless a constraint in the question rules it out.

recap.x: The whole subject in one table

head: The question says
Service
rows: Unpredictable relational load, or global failover in a minute
Aurora Serverless v2, or Aurora Global Database
SQL over files already in S3

recap.x: Known access patterns favour DynamoDB; unknown or ad-hoc queries favour a relational engine. That single question separates the two most common answers in this subject.
What each one is bad at

head: Service
Do not use it for
rows: Anything where the application cannot be changed
Workloads needing host access — use EC2 or RDS Custom

recap.x: Recurring distractors: DynamoDB proposed for a join-heavy application; Redshift proposed for transactions; a cache proposed when the application cannot change; and EC2-hosted databases proposed where a managed service would do.

final.q: A fraud team needs to find accounts connected to a suspicious account through shared devices, addresses and payment methods, within two or three hops. Which database fits?

o.w: Correct — multi-hop traversal across relationships is precisely what a graph database is optimised for.
A warehouse can express this as repeated joins but performs poorly and is aimed at aggregation.
Time series storage has no notion of relationships between entities.
Expressing traversals in a key-value store requires many round trips and careful key design.

final.x: "Connected through" and a hop count are the graph signals. Neptune supports Gremlin, openCypher and SPARQL, so the query language follows the team's existing skills.

final.q: A session store is read and written by session id millions of times per minute, with no reporting requirement. Which service is the best fit?

o.t: Neptune with a session vertex per user
o.w: A graph database adds relationship machinery this workload never uses.

o.t: DynamoDB, optionally with TTL to expire sessions
o.w: Correct — a single key-based access pattern at very high volume is DynamoDB's core case, and TTL removes expired sessions for free.
A warehouse is designed for analytical scans, not millions of point writes per minute.

o.t: RDS for PostgreSQL with read replicas
o.w: Replicas take read load but every write still goes to one primary, which becomes the bottleneck.

final.x: Known access pattern, extreme volume, no joins. DynamoDB's TTL also handles expiry without a cleanup job, which is why session stores are a textbook use of it.

final.q: A company runs a self-managed MongoDB cluster and wants to stop operating it while keeping its application code. Which service should it move to?

o.w: Moving to a relational engine would mean redesigning the document model.
DynamoDB has a different API and data model, making this a rewrite rather than a migration.
Correct — DocumentDB is MongoDB compatible, so existing drivers and queries continue to work.
Keyspaces is Cassandra compatible, which is a different wire protocol entirely.

final.x: Compatibility is the whole reason DocumentDB and Keyspaces exist. When a question names an open-source engine and says code should not change, the compatible managed service is the answer.

final.q: Analysts want SQL over ten terabytes of JSON logs already in S3, queried a few times a week. What is the most cost-effective option?

o.w: A key-value store cannot answer ad-hoc analytical SQL.
A relational instance would struggle with this volume and require a lengthy load.
A Redshift cluster is worth it for constant analytical load, not for a few queries a week.

o.t: Amazon Athena querying the data in place
o.w: Correct — Athena charges per data scanned and needs no cluster, which suits infrequent queries.

final.x: Query frequency is the deciding factor. Infrequent queries over data in S3 favour Athena; sustained heavy analytics justify a warehouse, and Redshift Spectrum bridges the two.

final.q: An industrial platform ingests millions of sensor readings per hour and reports averages per minute, hour and day. Which database is purpose-built for this?

o.w: Correct — Timestream stores time-stamped measurements with tiered storage and time-window query functions.
A relational engine can store this but becomes expensive and slow at this volume.
A document store has no time-series optimisations or built-in windowing.
A graph database models relationships, not measurement series.

final.x: The pairing of timestamped readings with window aggregations is the Timestream signature, and its memory-then-magnetic tiering is what makes long retention affordable.

final.q: A relational application must survive a regional outage with a recovery time of about one minute and minimal data loss. Which option meets it?

o.w: Global Tables are a key-value solution and would require abandoning the relational model.

o.t: Aurora Global Database with a secondary region
o.w: Correct — replication is typically under a second and a secondary region can be promoted in about a minute.

o.t: A nightly snapshot copied to another region
o.w: Nightly snapshots mean up to a day of data loss and a long restore.
Multi-AZ protects against zone failure, not the loss of an entire region.

final.x: The recovery time objective in minutes, on a relational workload, is Aurora Global Database's defining case. Multi-AZ and snapshots sit at very different points on that scale.

final.q: Which statement correctly characterises Amazon Redshift?

o.t: A key-value store with single-digit millisecond latency
o.w: That describes DynamoDB.

o.t: An in-memory cache for microsecond reads
o.w: That describes ElastiCache or DAX.

o.t: A columnar data warehouse for analytical queries, unsuited to high-volume single-row transactions
o.w: Correct — columnar storage and parallel processing favour large aggregations over point writes.
That describes DocumentDB.

final.x: Knowing what each service is *not* for eliminates options quickly. Redshift's columnar design is exactly why it excels at aggregation and struggles with transactional write patterns.

final.q: A DynamoDB-backed API is fast overall, but a handful of extremely popular items are read constantly and the team wants microsecond latency with minimal code change. What should be added?

o.t: A global secondary index on the popular items
o.w: An index creates a new access pattern; it does not cache anything.
Introducing a relational database as a cache is neither simple nor appropriate.
Redis would work but requires the application to implement cache population and invalidation.

o.t: A DAX cluster in front of the table
o.w: Correct — DAX is DynamoDB-aware, so adopting it is largely an endpoint change.

final.x: DAX exists for exactly this: hot-item read caching for DynamoDB with API compatibility, which is what makes it the low-change answer compared with a general-purpose cache.

final.q: A team must run a database engine version that AWS does not offer as a managed service, and needs operating system access for a vendor agent. What should they do?

o.t: Run the engine on EC2 and manage it themselves
o.w: Correct — an unsupported version plus host access rules out every managed relational option.

o.t: Use Aurora with a compatible engine
o.w: Aurora offers even less host access than RDS.

o.t: Use RDS with a custom parameter group
o.w: Parameter groups tune settings; they cannot provide an unsupported version or host access.

o.t: Use DynamoDB and adapt the schema
o.w: Changing data model to avoid an operational constraint is a rewrite, not a solution.

final.x: Managed services are the default answer, but two constraints override that: an engine or version AWS does not support, and a requirement for operating system access. RDS Custom covers some of this for Oracle and SQL Server.

final.q: An existing order system uses complex SQL joins across a dozen tables and must handle three times its current traffic. What is the most appropriate change?

o.t: Rewrite the data layer onto DynamoDB
o.w: A join-heavy application on a key-value store is a full redesign, not a scaling step.

o.t: Move to Aurora and scale reads with the reader endpoint
o.w: Correct — Aurora keeps the relational model while offering up to fifteen replicas and higher throughput.
A cache cannot replace the system of record.
Redshift is analytical and unsuited to transactional order processing.

final.x: Scaling a join-heavy relational workload is usually answered within the relational family: Aurora for throughput and replicas, plus a cache if reads dominate. Moving to DynamoDB is only right when the access patterns are simple and known.

A compressed copy of the data

When no cluster may be provisioned
When the data must stay in S3 untouched
For sustained, heavy analytical workloads with many concurrent users

o.w: Correct — CloudTrail records the identity, the API call, the time and the source IP.

final.x: CloudTrail is the audit trail of API activity. Config is the record of resource state — the two answer different halves of an investigation and are frequently confused.

final.q: Security wants an alert whenever the string "AuthenticationFailure" appears more than ten times in five minutes in an application log. What should be configured?

o.t: A Config rule matching the string
o.w: Config evaluates resource configuration, not log content.

o.t: A subscription filter delivering to SNS
o.w: Subscription filters stream events but do not evaluate thresholds.

o.t: A metric filter on the log group and a CloudWatch alarm on its metric
o.w: Correct — the filter turns matching log lines into a metric, and the alarm applies the threshold and period.
X-Ray traces requests and does not inspect log text.

final.x: Alarms only ever evaluate metrics, so anything in a log must first become a metric. Metric filters are the bridge, and they support counting occurrences of a pattern.

final.q: A nightly cleanup script runs on a small EC2 instance whose only purpose is cron. How should this be replaced?

o.w: Scheduled scaling changes capacity rather than running a task.
Alarms respond to metrics; they have no schedule of their own.

o.t: An AWS Config rule with remediation
o.w: Config rules evaluate compliance and are not a general scheduler.

o.t: An EventBridge scheduled rule invoking a Lambda function
o.w: Correct — scheduled rules provide cron semantics and invoke Lambda directly, removing the instance.

final.x: Replacing a cron server with an EventBridge schedule and Lambda is one of the standard serverless simplifications, provided the task fits within Lambda's limits.

final.q: A team must prove that every EBS volume in the account has been encrypted continuously for the last year, and be alerted if one is not. What provides this?

o.t: AWS Config with a managed rule and its configuration history
o.w: Correct — Config records configuration over time and continuously evaluates rules against it.
Trusted Advisor gives point-in-time checks without a full configuration history.

o.t: CloudWatch metric filters on the EC2 log group
o.w: Metric filters read log text and know nothing about volume configuration.
CloudTrail records the API calls but does not evaluate ongoing compliance state.

final.x: Continuous compliance with a historical record is Config's defining capability, and remediation actions can additionally fix violations automatically.

final.q: A customer-facing API intermittently takes several seconds, and the team cannot tell which downstream service is responsible. What should be added?

o.t: A CloudWatch dashboard of each service's CPU
o.w: Per-service metrics show symptoms without attributing a slow request to a hop.

o.t: AWS X-Ray tracing across the services
o.w: Correct — X-Ray traces a single request end to end and shows the latency of each segment.
Canaries detect outside failures but do not break a request into segments.
Conformance packs assess compliance, not latency.

final.x: Distributed tracing is the tool for "which hop is slow". Metrics tell you that something is slow; traces tell you where the time went within one request.

final.q: During an incident, twenty alarms fire simultaneously from a single database failure and the on-call channel becomes unusable. What is the appropriate change?

o.t: Raise every alarm threshold to reduce sensitivity
o.w: Raising thresholds hides real problems rather than organising the signal.

o.t: Switch the metrics to high resolution
o.w: Higher resolution produces more datapoints and, if anything, more alarms.

o.t: Create a composite alarm so one notification represents the underlying fault
o.w: Correct — composite alarms express a rule over other alarms and notify once for a root cause.

o.t: Move the alarms to a different SNS topic
o.w: Changing topics moves the noise without reducing it.

final.x: Composite alarms exist for exactly this: suppressing symptom alarms while still surfacing the failure, so that alerting stays actionable during an incident.

final.q: A team discovers that log storage costs have grown steadily since the account was created three years ago. What is the most likely cause and fix?

o.t: Detailed monitoring was left enabled; disable it
o.w: Detailed monitoring affects metric frequency and is not the source of log storage cost.

o.t: Metric filters are duplicating the logs; remove them
o.w: Metric filters read logs; they do not store additional copies.

o.t: Live Tail sessions are being billed; close them
o.w: Live Tail is a live view and does not accumulate storage.

o.t: Log groups default to never expiring; set retention periods and export what must be kept to S3
o.w: Correct — new log groups retain data indefinitely unless a retention period is configured.

final.x: Unbounded log retention is a quiet, compounding cost. Setting per-group retention, with an export to S3 and lifecycle rules for anything that must be kept, is the standard remedy.

final.q: An organisation with forty accounts must collect API activity from all of them into one place, with proof the records have not been altered. What should be configured?

o.t: An organization trail in CloudTrail with log file validation enabled, delivering to a central S3 bucket
o.w: Correct — an organization trail captures every member account, and log file validation proves integrity.
GuardDuty detects threats but is not an audit log.

o.t: AWS Config aggregators in each account
o.w: Config aggregates configuration state, not API activity.
Dashboards visualise metrics and do not collect audit records.

final.x: Organization trails plus log file validation is the standard multi-account audit design, usually paired with a locked-down central logging account.

final.q: A business requires notification within minutes if the public checkout page stops working, including overnight when there is little traffic. What detects this?

o.t: An EventBridge rule on EC2 state changes
o.w: Instance state changes say nothing about whether the checkout flow works.

o.t: A CloudWatch Synthetics canary running the checkout journey on a schedule
o.w: Correct — a canary exercises the journey from outside on a fixed schedule regardless of real traffic.

o.t: A metric filter on the web server logs
o.w: Log-based detection requires traffic to generate the logs.

o.t: A CloudWatch alarm on ALB request count
o.w: Request count alarms cannot distinguish a quiet night from an outage.

final.x: Synthetic monitoring is the answer whenever detection must not depend on real user traffic, which is exactly the overnight low-traffic case.
